To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

we designed and synthesized a decompressed genome that encodes the same proteins as bacteriophage ø174, we produced clonal preparations of the decompressed øX174. 1f genome in yeast vectors, and we recovered viable øX 174.1f phage particles in E. coli C cells.
we have assembled and archived a fully decompressed synthetic genome encoding the bacteriophage ø174 in yeast.
we have designed, synthesized and recovered viable bacteriophage ø174.1f particles containing a decompressed genome from E. Coli C cells that independently express full length gene F.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the development of a new platform for the design, synthesis, and assembly of synthetic genomes.
the development of yeast as an archival and manipulative platform for the maintenance of synthetic genomes.
the development of yeast as a repository for synthetic phage genomes.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
yeast can serve a genomic 'dry dock' for maintaining and manipulating clonal lineages for obligate lytic bacteriophages.
we have demonstrated the utility of yeast as a genomic drydock for the maintenance and manipulation of clonal lineages for a wide variety of obligate lytic bacteriophage.
we have demonstrated a proof of concept for the assembly and storage of a synthetic phage genome in yeast.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that yeast can serve a genomic 'dry dock' for maintaining and manipulating clonal lineages for other lytic phages.
we have demonstrated that it is possible to fully decompress the genome of a small bacteriophage in yeast and recover viable progeny phage.
we have demonstrated that a synthetic bacteriophage genome can be assembled in yeast and that the resulting recombinant yeast plasmid is stable.
The main takeaway from our work is that
yeast can serve to archive, manipulate, and express a fully synthetic bacteriophage genome.
yeast can be engineered to maintain clonal lineages encoding a fully decompressed bacteriophage ø genome.
yeast can serve to maintain and manipulate the clonal lineages for other obligate lytical phage.
